prompt: When the lab comes up, remote reaches the database on db. Why?
hint: Look at what fw was doing before any rule was typed.

choices.text: The database had a weak password
choices.why: No password was involved: the connection opened before any login.

choices.text: fw routed the packets and asked nothing about them
choices.why: Right. Routing delivers; filtering is the separate question nobody had asked yet.

choices.text: remote exploited a flaw in the router firmware to slip past it
choices.why: Nothing was broken. The router did exactly what a router does.

choices.text: db was in the DMZ
choices.why: db is on the servers segment, 192.168.20.0/24.

prompt: Match each packet to the nftables hook on fw that sees it.
hint: Is fw the destination, the source, or neither?

pairs.left: admin opening SSH to fw itself
fw asking the DNS server for a name

prompt: Why does a rule on fw test the interface a packet arrived on, and not only its source address?
hint: Who writes each of the two?

choices.text: Interfaces are faster to match than addresses, which matters under load
choices.why: Speed is not the reason; both are cheap.

choices.text: An address cannot be written in an nftables rule
choices.why: ip saddr and ip daddr are in the rules of this very lesson.

choices.text: The sender fills in the source field; the wiring decides the other
choices.why: Right. A source address is a claim; the interface is a fact about the path.

choices.text: Addresses change every time the lab is reset
choices.why: The lab's addresses are fixed.

prompt: Source and destination address, protocol, and source and destination port together are called the ___-tuple.
hint: Count them.

prompt: With only the rule for dport 8080 loaded, curl from laptop ended with exit 28. What happened?
hint: Two packets travel for every request: which one had a rule?

choices.text: The request was dropped by fw on its way over to app
choices.why: The request matched the rule and reached app.

choices.text: The reply had no rule
choices.why: Right. A stateless filter treats the reply as just another packet.

choices.text: app refused the connection because nothing listened there
choices.why: A refusal comes back at once; exit 28 is a timeout.

choices.text: curl could not resolve the server's name into an address
choices.why: The request used an address, not a name.

prompt: A stateless rule set must allow the LAN to reach three different services on the servers segment, and nothing else. How many accept rules does it need?
hint: One per direction, per service.

prompt: What does policy drop on the forward chain decide?
hint: It is the chain's last word.

choices.text: That every packet is dropped, whatever the rules say
choices.why: A rule that accepts ends the matter before the policy.

choices.text: That packets addressed to fw itself are dropped
choices.why: Those are input, not forward.

choices.text: The verdict for what no rule accepted
choices.why: Right. It is what happens after the last rule.

choices.text: That dropped packets are logged
choices.why: Logging needs a rule of its own.

prompt: From db, nc -p 8080 reached laptop's port 9999 through the stateless rules. What made that possible?
hint: Who chooses a source port?

choices.text: A flaw in nc that forges the packet's headers
choices.why: nc only asked the system for a source port, which any program may do.

choices.text: The return rule matches any sport 8080
choices.why: Right. It was written for replies and cannot tell a reply from anything else.

choices.text: db is on the LAN side, so no rule applied to it
choices.why: db is on the servers segment and crossed fw.

choices.text: The chain's policy was accept rather than drop
choices.why: The first attempt, without -p 8080, was dropped.

prompt: Which stateless return rules let in more than replies? Choose all that apply.
hint: A port number is written by the sender.

choices.text: tcp sport 80 accept
choices.why: Any connection from port 80 to any port inside.

choices.text: udp sport 53 accept
choices.why: Any datagram claiming a DNS server's port.

choices.text: tcp sport 8080 accept
choices.why: The rule this lesson watched db walk through.

choices.text: ct state established accept
choices.why: That one is stateful: it matches only conversations already allowed.

prompt: A stateless ACL adds a check that the TCP flags look like a reply. What does that still fail to establish?
hint: What would it have to remember?

choices.text: Whether the packet is TCP at all, rather than UDP or ICMP
choices.why: Testing flags already implies TCP.

choices.text: Which interface the packet arrived on and which it will leave by
choices.why: Interfaces can be tested without state.

choices.text: Whether the destination port is open
choices.why: No firewall rule knows that.

choices.text: That the packet belongs to a conversation it allowed
choices.why: Right. Flags describe one packet; belonging needs a memory of conversations.

prompt: Match each conntrack state to the packet it describes.
hint: Four states, and one description belongs to none.

pairs.right: the first packet of a conversation not yet in the table
a packet of a conversation already in the table
an ICMP error about a known conversation
an acknowledgement for a connection never seen

right_distractors: a packet the firewall has decided to log

prompt: In the stateful rule set, which rule replaces every return rule?
hint: It is the first one.

choices.text: ct state established,related accept
choices.why: Right. Replies of every allowed conversation, in both directions.

choices.text: ct state invalid drop
choices.why: That throws away what belongs to nothing.

choices.text: policy drop
choices.why: That is what happens to everything left.

choices.text: ct state new accept
choices.why: That decides which conversations may start.

prompt: The open connection's conntrack entry showed 431999 seconds left. About how many days is the full timeout of 432000 seconds?
hint: Divide by 86,400.

prompt: Why does a conntrack entry store the reply direction as well as the original one?
hint: What is a packet from app compared against?

choices.text: To keep a separate log line for each direction of the traffic
choices.why: Logging is not what the table is for.

choices.text: So a returning packet is matched to the conversation
choices.why: Right. The second tuple is exactly what a reply must look like.

choices.text: Because TCP needs two connections, one per direction
choices.why: One TCP connection carries both directions.

choices.text: To count bytes in each direction for billing
choices.why: Counting is possible, but it is not why the tuple is there.

prompt: A conversation's first packet is dropped by the policy. What does conntrack remember of it afterwards?
hint: An entry is made when a rule accepts.

choices.text: An entry marked invalid
choices.why: invalid is a verdict about a packet, not an entry.

choices.text: An entry that expires after 30 seconds
choices.why: No entry was made to expire.

choices.text: Nothing: no entry was created
choices.why: Right. So its replies have nothing to match.

choices.text: An entry held until the connection times out
choices.why: A dropped packet leaves nothing in the table.

prompt: dig asked app, which runs no DNS, and printed connection refused at once. Which rule let the answer through?
hint: The answer was an ICMP message about the query.

choices.text: ct state established accept
choices.why: Its counter moved for the reply from the real DNS server, not this.

choices.text: ct state related accept
choices.why: Right. An ICMP port unreachable about a known flow is related.

choices.text: The rule allowing udp dport 53 to app
choices.why: That rule matches only new packets towards app.

choices.text: The policy
choices.why: The policy is drop.

prompt: What goes wrong if related is not accepted? Choose all that apply.
hint: Think of the ICMP messages that report a problem.

choices.text: Programs wait for a timeout instead of failing at once
choices.why: The refusal never arrives.

choices.text: A sender never learns its packets are too big
choices.why: That message is related too, and connections stall.

choices.text: Established connections are dropped
choices.why: established is a separate state with its own rule.

choices.text: New connections from the LAN are refused
choices.why: new is decided by its own rule.

prompt: After loading the counted rule set, remote tried the database once. How many packets did the last counter record?
hint: The first try and one retransmission.

prompt: Why is ct state established,related the first rule of the chain?
hint: Look at the counters after three requests.

choices.text: Nearly every packet matches it, so the others are rarely tested
choices.why: Right. 34 packets there against 3 on the new rule.

choices.text: nftables refuses a chain whose first rule is something else
choices.why: Any order loads; the order changes cost and meaning.

choices.text: It must come before the policy is read
choices.why: The policy applies after the last rule, wherever this one sits.

choices.text: Rules below it are skipped for new packets
choices.why: A new packet falls past it to the rules below.

prompt: A single DNS question and its answer pass through fw. How long does conntrack keep the flow if nothing else arrives?
hint: It is the shorter UDP value.

choices.text: Five days
choices.why: That is for an established TCP connection.

choices.text: 120 seconds
choices.why: That is for a UDP stream, with traffic back and forth.

choices.text: 30 seconds
choices.why: Right. nf_conntrack_udp_timeout = 30.

choices.text: Until the table is full
choices.why: Every entry has a timeout.

prompt: Match each place to the kind of filter it fits.
hint: Memory costs; which places cannot afford it or do not need it?

pairs.left: a border router with millions of flows
pairs.right: stateless, dropping what can never be legitimate

pairs.left: the firewall deciding which conversations may start
a switch matching headers in hardware
pairs.right: an ACL that keeps no table

right_distractors: a WAF reading the HTTP request

prompt: A Linux firewall restarts in the middle of the day. What happens to a TCP connection that was open through it, with the default settings shown in the lesson?
hint: nf_conntrack_tcp_loose = 1.

choices.text: It is dropped as invalid on its next packet
choices.why: That is what a stricter firewall does, with loose off.

choices.text: It is picked up as new and a fresh entry made
choices.why: Right, if a rule allows it as new: Linux adopts mid-stream TCP by default.

choices.text: The entry survives the restart, saved to disk beforehand
choices.why: The table lives in memory.

choices.text: The client is told to reconnect by fw
choices.why: fw sends nothing of the kind.

prompt: An audit finds a router ACL with the rule permit tcp any eq 443 any, meant for replies from web servers. Which change closes what it opens without breaking the replies?
hint: The lesson's fix for the same shape.

choices.text: Change 443 to a port above 1024
choices.why: Any number the sender may choose has the same problem.

choices.text: Log the rule and review the log weekly
choices.why: Logging watches the hole; it does not close it.

choices.text: Move the filtering to a stateful firewall that accepts established traffic and allows only the outgoing connections
choices.why: Right. Replies then pass because they belong to a conversation, not because of a number.

choices.text: Add a second rule for port 80
choices.why: That doubles the hole.

prompt: With the stateful rule set of this lesson, admin tries to open SSH to app. What happens?
hint: Which rule lets a conversation start?

choices.text: It is dropped
choices.why: Right. Only the LAN, to app on 8080, may start a conversation; admin is on mgmt.

choices.text: It passes, because SSH is encrypted and fw cannot read it
choices.why: The rules read headers, and encryption does not hide the port.

choices.text: It passes as established after the first packet
choices.why: The first packet is new and nothing accepts it, so there is no entry.

choices.text: fw answers with connection refused
choices.why: A drop sends nothing back; the client times out.

prompt: Put in order what happens to laptop's first packet to app on 8080 under the stateful rule set.
hint: Conntrack looks before the rules do.
items: conntrack finds no entry and marks the packet new
the established,related rule does not match
the new rule for the LAN to app on 8080 accepts it
an entry is created for its replies to match
trap: The entry exists only once a rule has accepted the new packet.
